fields.features_heading: Inside Every Food Quiz Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Describe the quiz once. Emergent builds the questions and the result screens, plus a table that catches every answer.
fields.feature_1:
Matched or graded, from the same prompt

Say which way the quiz ends: every option can point to a result, or an answer key can score it. Emergent builds either from one prompt and rewrites any question you name.
fields.feature_2:
Result screens with a next step

Each result names what happens after the last question: the dish to order, the practice set to open, or the list to join. Edit any result screen by describing the change.
fields.feature_3:
Every answer lands in your table

Each finished quiz writes a row in a table you own: the picks, the result, and the time it came in. Filter by result before a menu change or before a classroom retake.
fields.feature_4:
Email capture synced through any API

An email step after the result screen saves each address beside its result, and the app syncs both into any tool with an API, from a mailing list to a CRM you already run.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen, no caps

Takers answer one question per screen on a phone, and Emergent puts no response cap on the quiz, so a round that spreads past your own crowd keeps counting every finish.
fields.feature_6:
The code comes with you

Export the full code of the quiz to your GitHub repository on paid plans, rerun it next season, or hand it to a developer. The quiz you built this year stays yours to run.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Teams Put a Food Quiz to Work
fields.tab_content_1:
The kitchen reads 412 matches and picks one special

Mirela Stanchev takes the menu match quiz on Peppervine Taqueria's site and lands on Al Pastor. October closes with 412 finished quizzes: 158 Al Pastor, 121 Barbacoa, 83 Rajas, and 50 Chorizo. The kitchen reads the split and runs Al Pastor as the weekend special, with every pick saved to the menu table.
fields.tab_content_2:
Question 9 misses its mark and leaves the round

Copper Kettle Taproom scores its 15-question food round live for 12 teams on Thursday nights. Question 9 stumps 10 of the 12; the host swaps it before next week. The Thyme Bandits take the night with 13 of 15, and every team's sheet lands in the rounds table before the bar closes.
fields.tab_content_3:
Whole grains, missed by 17, get a second pass

Rosalind Achebe's class of 24 takes a food groups quiz on classroom tablets, and it grades itself as each student finishes. Question 6, on whole grains, is missed by 17 of 24. Monday opens with a second pass at the topic, and every score under 7 of 10 comes with a practice set attached.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every captured email carries its cooking style

Supper Trail's weeknight cooking style quiz closes the month at 1,240 finishes, and 744 takers leave an email at the result screen. The app tags each address with its result, 520 Pan Minimalist, 430 Batch Planner, and 290 Slow Simmerer, and syncs the tagged list to the brand's mailing tool.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Food Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to make a food quiz that matches a taste or totals a score, then build it on Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the result screen serves
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the results before the questions
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Map each option or set the answer key
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the ending before anything else: a matched dish for a menu, a graded score for a class or a game night, or a style that feeds a mailing list. Every question you write afterward has to point at that ending.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write 3 to 5 results first, each with a name, 2 lines of description, and a next step someone can take tonight. If a result cannot suggest anything, cut it and fold its answers into one that can.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Keep a food quiz between 6 and 10 questions, and make each one a single choice, like crunchy or creamy, or mild or on fire. Skip anything a taker has to research; the fun is in answering fast.
fields.howto_step_4_des: For a matched quiz, point every option at one result and check that each result is reachable. For a graded one, mark the correct option and set the score bands, like a practice set under 7 of 10.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Build it on Emergent from one prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Describe the quiz in plain English, from the questions and the results down to the table that collects every answer. Emergent builds the whole thing, and a follow-up prompt renames a result or swaps a question.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Take it 3 times before anyone else
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run one pass per ending you expect: the match you predicted, the top score, the worst score. Read each result screen as a stranger would, and fix any ending that lands wrong before the quiz leaves your desk.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Publish it and read the table
fields.howto_step_7_des: Share the link, then watch the rows come in: results and scores, plus emails if you ask for them. Swap the question everyone misses, retire a result nobody lands on, and run the next round with a sharper quiz.

faq_plan.a: A food quiz is a short set of questions about taste or food knowledge that ends on a result. One kind matches each taker to something, a dish, a style, a recipe list; the other grades answers against a key and shows a score.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a food quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in plain English in Emergent's AI survey builder: the questions plus the results or the answer key. Everything is built from that one prompt, and you change any piece, a question, an ending, the table, by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a food quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Six to 10 is the range to aim for. Keep food quiz questions to single choices a taker can answer in seconds, and cut any question that does not change which result someone lands on.

faq_plan.q: How do I make a food quiz for kids?
faq_plan.a: Shorten everything: a food quiz for kids runs best at 6 questions with 3 choices each, written at the grade level you teach. End on results that name something to try at dinner, not a grade. The same one-screen-at-a-time format carries a fitness quiz when field day comes around.

faq_plan.q: Can I use food quiz questions and answers I already have?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Paste the food quiz questions and answers you already use into the prompt, and the quiz is built around them, with each option mapped or marked correct as you wrote it. Emergent also drafts new questions in the same pass when your set runs short.

faq_plan.q: What are good food quiz questions?
faq_plan.hint: What are good food quiz questions?
faq_plan.a: Single choices with personality: pick a condiment to defend forever, name the dish you would order twice, or choose between crunchy and creamy. For a graded round, use questions with one checkable answer, like which cuisine a dish belongs to, and keep anything debatable out of the key.

faq_plan.q: Should a food quiz have right answers or matched results?
faq_plan.a: Grade it when a score is the point, for a classroom or a game night; match it when the ending is a recommendation, like a dish or a cooking style. The matching format is the same engine that runs a personality quiz: every option nudges the taker toward one result.

faq_plan.q: Can a food quiz recommend dishes from a menu?
faq_plan.a: Yes. List the dishes as results, point each answer option toward one of them, and the last screen names a dish to order. On Emergent the menu lives in a table you own, and swapping a dish means editing a row, not rebuilding the quiz.

faq_plan.q: Can I collect emails with a food quiz?
faq_plan.a: Yes, and the result screen is the place to ask, after someone has a reason to want the recipe list or the next round's date. Each address saves beside its result, and no response cap cuts the list short in a busy week.

faq_plan.q: What should the end of a food quiz show?
faq_plan.a: Three things: the result's name, one line on why the answers point there, and a next step, the dish to try, the practice set, or the signup. The same scoring that picks a result here powers a spirit animal quiz, where every answer adds a point toward one animal.

quiz.title: What Is Your Food Style?
quiz.intro: Eight quick picks about what you cook, order, and crave. Finish and you get one of four food styles, with a dinner idea to match.

questions.text: It is Friday night and the kitchen is yours. What goes on the stove?

options.text: A stew that takes all evening
A stir fry with serious heat
A big salad with a fried egg on top
Pancakes, because nobody can stop you

questions.text: Choose the condiment you reach for first.
You open a menu at a new spot. Where do your eyes go?

options.text: The dish the place is known for

questions.text: What does your ideal breakfast look like?
A potluck invite lands. What do you bring?

options.text: A salsa with a warning label
A grain salad with herbs from your pot

questions.text: Choose a kitchen tool you could not give up.

options.text: The cast iron skillet, screaming hot
A quick market run and a 10 minute saute

questions.text: Pick a snack for a road trip.

options.text: A bakery cookie the size of your hand

results.title: The Comfort Classic
results.description: Your answers lean toward the dishes that never miss: the stew, the roast, and the mac and cheese with the crackly top. You cook what you already love, and you make it a little better every time. Dinner idea to match: a slow braise on Sunday, with enough left over to make Monday easy.

results.title: The Heat Seeker
results.description: Your answers lean toward the end of the menu marked with a pepper. You order the special, you ask for the hotter version, and your pantry holds three kinds of chili crisp. Dinner idea to match: a weeknight stir fry built around whatever makes your forehead glow.

results.title: The Garden Grazer
results.description: Your answers lean toward what is fresh right now: the market tomato, the herb you grew yourself, the salad people actually finish. You cook light and let the ingredients do the talking. Dinner idea to match: a grain bowl with a fried egg and whatever the produce drawer offers.

results.title: The Sweet Finisher
results.description: Your answers lean toward the end of the meal, because that is the part you plan first. You read the dessert menu before you pick a main, and your oven sees more cookies than casseroles. Dinner idea to match: breakfast for dinner, pancakes included.
